summary.text: For \(k>59\), set \(n=2k+1\); a nonzero determinant forces the matrix to have a nonzero entry, which supplies two primes symmetric about \(n\) and hence summing to \(2n=4k+2\). The remaining cases \(1\le k\le59\) are established by explicit prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the determinant defining A228623. Thus, for a positive integer \(n\), let
\[
M_n=(m_{ij})_{0\le i,j<n}
\]
be the \(n\times n\) integer matrix whose entries are
\[
m_{ij}=\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the subtractions are natural-number subtractions. Because \(0\le i,j<n\), neither subtraction truncates past zero: indeed \(j<n\le n+i\) and \(i<n\le n+j\). The sequence term is
\[
a(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement:
\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne0.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that, for every positive integer \(k\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

We first record the elementary consequence of the determinant definition that drives the argument. Suppose \(n>0\) and \(a(n)\ne0\). Then at least one entry of \(M_n\) is nonzero. Otherwise every entry would be zero, so \(M_n\) would be the zero \(n\times n\) matrix; since \(n>0\), its determinant is zero, contrary to \(a(n)\ne0\). Every entry of \(M_n\) is either zero or one, so there are indices \(i,j\), with
\[
0\le i<n,\qquad 0\le j<n,
\]
for which \(m_{ij}=1\). By the definition of the matrix, the two natural numbers
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\tag{2}
\]
are both prime.

Moreover, these primes satisfy
\[
p+q=2n.
\tag{3}
\]
To justify this identity despite the use of natural-number subtraction, observe again that \(j\le n+i\) and \(i\le n+j\). Thus both differences in (2) are exact differences, rather than truncated differences. We may consequently calculate in the integers and then return to the natural numbers:
\[
(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n+i+j-j-i=2n.
\]
This proves (3). We have therefore established the following intermediate result:

> If \(n>0\) and \(a(n)\ne0\), then \(2n\) is a sum of two primes.

Now fix an integer \(k>0\). We divide the proof into a finite small case and the range where hypothesis (1) applies.

### The range \(1\le k\le59\)

Every summand displayed in this table is prime. This is a direct finite primality check. More explicitly, apart from the immediately prime numbers \(3,5,7,11,13\), all displayed summands belong to
\[
\begin{split}
\{&19,23,31,37,43,47,53,59,61,67,71,73,79,83,89,97,103,107,109,113,\\
&127,131,139,151,157,163,167,173,179,181,191,193,199,211,223,227,229,233\}.
\end{split}
\]
For each number in this set, trial division by primes not exceeding its square root shows that it has no proper prime divisor. Since every number is at most \(233\), it is enough to test \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), omitting a proposed divisor when it is not below the number in question; none divides any of the listed numbers. Thus the table proves the desired assertion throughout \(1\le k\le59\).

### The range \(k>59\)

Since \(k\) is integral, this means \(k\ge60\). Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge 2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
Hypothesis (1) therefore gives
\[
a(n)\ne0.
\]
Also \(n>0\). By the intermediate determinant consequence proved above, there are indices \(0\le i,j<n\) such that
\[
p=n+i-j\quad\text{and}\quad q=n+j-i
\]
are prime and satisfy \(p+q=2n\). Substituting \(n=2k+1\) gives
\[
p+q=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Thus \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes in this range as well.

The two cases cover every positive integer \(k\). Hence the conjecture that \(a(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\) implies that every integer of the form \(4k+2\), with \(k>0\), is the sum of two primes.
